claims.text: The initial material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing L12/FCC-like and B2 phases.
The L12 phase is more corrosion resistant than the B2 phase.
Elevated temperature destabilizes the passive film of the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type alloy in chloride-containing sulfuric acid.
The B2 phase is preferentially susceptible to pitting and dissolution in chloride-containing acidic solution.
Cyclic mechanical contact periodically removes the transient oxide film.
Mechanical oxide removal occurs preferentially over the B2 phase.
Mechanical exposure of the B2 phase initiates localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion further destabilizes the worn surface and prevents uniform oxide-film regeneration.
Repetitive wear and transient passivation breakdown produce synergistic degradation beyond the separately imposed wear and corrosion responses.
Abrasive and oxidative wear can predominate in an AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy-alloy coating.
Stabilizing a passive film through compositional modification can improve corrosion resistance.
Relative to a stabilized-film baseline, simultaneous wear and corrosion will cause greater total material loss.
Relative to the baseline, the wear rate will increase because the oxide film is frequently removed.
Relative to the baseline, the corrosion rate will increase because of localized pitting and dissolution on the vulnerable phase.
The mechanism is expected to operate at 100–300 °C in chloride-containing acidic media under contact stresses sufficient to disrupt the oxide.
The mechanism should not operate when the oxide film remains inherently stable or when mechanical loading cannot disrupt it.
Comparing natural film formation with a stabilized-film control under otherwise identical tribocorrosion conditions can distinguish the proposed mechanism.
A lack of a significant wear or corrosion difference, or failure to observe cyclic film rupture and phase-localized pitting, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
